photon-energy.label: Vacuum wavelength λ
photon-energy.description: A light-source designer compares photons from ideal monochromatic emitters. Change the vacuum wavelength λ in nanometres. The wave spacing marks that physical length on a fixed ruler; the energy bar independently measures the energy carried by one photon.

photon-energy.label: Photon energy and vacuum wavelength primary result
photon-energy.description: For an ideal monochromatic photon in vacuum, frequency f and wavelength λ satisfy fλ=c, and photon energy in joules is E_J=hf. The speed of light c and Planck constant h have exact SI defining values. Divide the joule reading by the exact conversion u=1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ joules per electronvolt to obtain its electronvolt reading E. Shorter wavelength gives higher frequency and higher energy per photon; it does not by itself specify beam brightness or power.

time-dilation.label: Relative speed fraction β
time-dilation.description: An ideal coasting spacecraft clock marks a start event and a finish event. Choose its proper elapsed time τ and its speed fraction β relative to a laboratory. Compare the clock interval with the laboratory coordinate interval for those same two events, using one fixed seconds ruler.

time-dilation.label: Clock proper interval τ
time-dilation.description: An ideal coasting spacecraft clock marks a start event and a finish event. Choose its proper elapsed time τ and its speed fraction β relative to a laboratory. Compare the clock interval with the laboratory coordinate interval for those same two events, using one fixed seconds ruler.

time-dilation.label: Time dilation between two clock events primary result
time-dilation.description: For two events at the same position in the rest frame of an ideal inertial clock, its proper elapsed time is τ. A laboratory inertial frame in which that clock moves with speed v assigns coordinate interval t=γτ, where β=v/c and γ=1/√(1−β²). The two events generally occupy different laboratory positions. The factor γ is at least one, and equals one when relative speed is zero.
